> **Core finding.** On IFLA's standard public-library metric frame, Delhi Public
> Library is not merely smaller than Toronto Public Library. It is operating at
> a different order of public reach. Using the NCT service-area denominator of
> 19.0 million residents, DPL records about **14,461 annual book issues per
> million residents**. TPL records about **9.33 million borrowings per million
> residents**. That is a **645x per-capita use gap**.

## Denominator

The primary denominator is **NCT of Delhi**, not the full National Capital
Region. DPL is treated as a Delhi service-area institution; comparing it to the
full NCR would charge it for a wider regional population it does not formally
cover. NCR is still useful as a latent-demand sensitivity, because readers and
workers cross the NCT boundary, but it is not the headline denominator.

The old 2011-only denominator is not used for the main comparison. SevenT4 now
uses the `theright2read` population correction source: `STATE_POP_MN["Delhi"] =
19`, which cites the MoHFW Technical Group population projections for 2011-2036.
The exact annual Delhi row should still be promoted when the source PDF is
reachable; the MoHFW server timed out during this session.

| Area | Population used | Role |
|---|---:|---|
| NCT of Delhi | 19,000,000 | Primary DPL service-area denominator |
| City of Toronto | 3,000,000 | Primary TPL service-area denominator |
| NCR sensitivity | 27,000,000-32,000,000 | Latent-demand sensitivity only |

## IFLA Frame

This report uses the IFLA Library Map of the World metric frame: service points,
registered users, physical visits, physical loans, eBook loans, audio-book
loans, downloads, staff, volunteers, and libraries with internet access. The
comparison below uses only fields that are currently captured from source
reports. Missing IFLA fields are listed as data gaps rather than inferred.

| IFLA-aligned metric | DPL, NCT baseline | TPL, city baseline | Reading |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Conservative service points per 1M | 2.1 | 34.0 | TPL has 16.2x the service-point density. |
| Inclusive DPL touchpoints per 1M | 8.6 | 34.0 | Even counting DPL mobile stops and reading centres, TPL is 4.0x denser. |
| Registered users per 1M | 5,818 | Not published in current TPL source | DPL has about one registered member per 172 NCT residents. |
| New card registrations per 1M | Not comparable | 78,423 | TPL reports new registrations, not total registered users. |
| Physical loans / borrowings per 1M | 14,461 | 9,333,333 | TPL is 645x higher per resident. |
| Physical visits proxy per 1M | 17,646 | 4,466,667 | DPL reports reading-room attendance, not all visits; TPL is 253x higher. |
| Collection items per 1M | 80,396 | 3,500,000 | TPL has 43.5x the collection density. |
| Annual additions per 1M | 164 | Not captured | DPL collection refresh is only 0.20%. |

The most important warning is not simply that DPL has fewer outlets. It is that
use is extremely low relative to both population and collection stock. DPL
records **0.18 annual issues per collection item**. TPL records about **2.67
borrowings per collection item**. That is a 14.8x stock-turnover gap.

## Finance

PPP conversion uses the World Bank `PA.NUS.PPP` indicator: India 2024 at
20.4219876045922 INR per international dollar, and Canada 2025 at 1.147294 CAD
per international dollar.

| Finance metric | DPL | TPL |
|---|---:|---:|
| Operating expenditure, PPP | $16.11m intl. | $258.05m intl. |
| Operating spend per resident, PPP | $0.85 | $86.02 |
| Spend per loan / borrowing, PPP | $58.63 | $9.22 |
| Materials expenditure, PPP | $0.086m intl. | $20.12m intl. |
| Materials spend per resident, PPP | $0.0045 | $6.71 |
| Materials share of expenditure | 0.53% | 7.80% |

The finance interpretation is straightforward:

- TPL operates at 16.0x DPL's PPP expenditure scale.
- TPL spends 101.5x more per resident.
- DPL's low captured use makes spend per loan high despite low total funding.
- TPL's materials spending is over 230x DPL's PPP materials line and 1,481x
  higher per resident.
- DPL is not renewing or circulating stock at TPL-like intensity.

DPL's 2023-24 inflow is almost entirely grant-funded: grant receipts are
97.99% of grant plus other income, while other income is 2.01%. That is not a
problem by itself; public libraries are public goods. The problem is that the
public subsidy is not translating into visible public use.

DPL also ended 2023-24 with **INR 4.78 crore** in closing unspent balance. That
is **14.5% of annual expenditure** and **27.2x the annual books and reading
materials expense**. In a network with 49.6% staff vacancy and a 0.20% collection
refresh rate, the unspent balance is operationally important.

## DPL Timeline

The DPL extraction now emits the full online annual-report panel from 2009-10
through 2023-24. The online DPL source package contains annual reports for every
year in that span; 2012-13, 2016-17, and 2020-21 required OCR recovery because
the original `pdftotext` output was image-only or mostly blank.

| Year | Members | Issues | Issues per 1M | Attendance | Collection | Additions | Refresh |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2009-10 | 64,883 | 1,039,977 | 54,736 | 316,657 | 1,552,000 | 77,872 | 5.02% |
| 2010-11 | 73,467 | 1,169,734 | 61,565 | 244,499 | 1,608,813 | 33,868 | 2.10% |
| 2011-12 | 76,548 | 1,133,154 | 59,640 | 477,107 | 1,640,909 | 39,860 | 2.43% |
| 2012-13 | 80,448 | 1,138,767 | 59,935 | 398,029 | 1,681,426 | 40,517 | 2.41% |
| 2013-14 | 107,276 | 1,081,767 | 56,935 | 397,718 | 1,694,695 | 23,565 | 1.39% |
| 2014-15 | 126,091 | 845,044 | 44,476 | 384,049 | 1,668,258 | 59,570 | 3.57% |
| 2015-16 | 139,835 | 757,439 | 39,865 | 314,089 | 1,717,727 | 37,014 | 2.16% |
| 2016-17 | 159,200 | 700,412 | 36,864 | 293,883 | 1,706,326 | 38,256 | 2.24% |
| 2017-18 | 175,422 | 730,706 | 38,458 | 330,888 | 1,735,868 | 21,545 | 1.24% |
| 2018-19 | 187,138 | 814,858 | 42,887 | 365,854 | 1,694,950 | 27,958 | 1.65% |
| 2019-20 | 189,235 | 477,008 | 25,106 | 353,246 | 1,596,125 | 13,310 | 0.83% |
| 2020-21 | 165,854 | 112,946 | 5,945 | 25,855 | 1,602,290 | 2,504 | 0.16% |
| 2021-22 | 156,867 | 196,889 | 10,363 | 132,411 | 1,605,443 | 2,697 | 0.17% |
| 2022-23 | 148,094 | 258,180 | 13,588 | 328,728 | 1,536,905 | 9,947 | 0.65% |
| 2023-24 | 110,534 | 274,751 | 14,461 | 335,270 | 1,527,531 | 3,108 | 0.20% |

The full online-run trend is severe. From 2009-10 to 2023-24, annual issues fall
from 1,039,977 to 274,751, a 73.6% decline. Books added fall from 77,872 to
3,108, a 96.0% decline. Collection stock is roughly flat, moving from 1.55m to
1.53m items, so the collapse is not explained by a shrinking collection.

The peak-to-latest trend is sharper on active reach. Membership peaks at 189,235
in 2019-20 and falls to 110,534 in 2023-24, a 41.6% decline. Issues peak at
1.17m in 2010-11 and fall to 274,751 in 2023-24, a 76.5% decline.

Reading-room attendance is the one partial recovery signal: 2023-24 attendance
is back near the 2017-18 to 2019-20 range. But reading-room recovery does not
offset the collapse in issue activity and stock renewal.

## Annual Toronto Comparison

For the annual comparison, DPL fiscal years are aligned to the TPL calendar year
matching the DPL fiscal end year. TPL open data covers 2012-2023; DPL 2023-24 is
compared to TPL's 2024 headline public metrics.

| DPL year | TPL year | DPL issues per 1M | TPL borrowings per 1M | TPL/DPL ratio | DPL attendance per 1M | TPL branch visits per 1M | TPL/DPL visit ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2009-10 | 2010 | 54,736 | Not available | Not available | 16,666 | Not available | Not available |
| 2010-11 | 2011 | 61,565 | Not available | Not available | 12,868 | Not available | Not available |
| 2011-12 | 2012 | 59,640 | 10,677,345 | 179.0x | 25,111 | 6,290,871 | 250.5x |
| 2012-13 | 2013 | 59,935 | 10,715,007 | 178.8x | 20,949 | 6,161,798 | 294.1x |
| 2013-14 | 2014 | 56,935 | 10,678,265 | 187.6x | 20,933 | 6,111,977 | 292.0x |
| 2014-15 | 2015 | 44,476 | 10,835,321 | 243.6x | 20,213 | 6,051,026 | 299.4x |
| 2015-16 | 2016 | 39,865 | 10,636,859 | 266.8x | 16,531 | 6,077,456 | 367.6x |
| 2016-17 | 2017 | 36,864 | 10,032,963 | 272.2x | 15,468 | 5,790,011 | 374.3x |
| 2017-18 | 2018 | 38,458 | 10,185,190 | 264.8x | 17,415 | 5,859,124 | 336.4x |
| 2018-19 | 2019 | 42,887 | 10,220,678 | 238.3x | 19,256 | 5,749,587 | 298.6x |
| 2019-20 | 2020 | 25,106 | 7,000,305 | 278.8x | 18,592 | 1,852,584 | 99.6x |
| 2020-21 | 2021 | 5,945 | 8,076,365 | 1,358.6x | 1,361 | 1,343,163 | 987.0x |
| 2021-22 | 2022 | 10,363 | 8,866,311 | 855.6x | 6,969 | 3,188,829 | 457.6x |
| 2022-23 | 2023 | 13,588 | 8,330,966 | 613.1x | 17,302 | 4,169,274 | 241.0x |
| 2023-24 | 2024 | 14,461 | 9,333,333 | 645.4x | 17,646 | 4,466,667 | 253.1x |

This comparison shows that the gap is not a one-year artefact. Before COVID,
TPL already records roughly 179x-278x DPL's per-capita borrowing. After the DPL
collapse in 2020-21, the ratio remains above 600x in the latest two comparable
years.

## NCR Sensitivity

If the full NCR population range of 27-32 million is used as a shadow catchment,
the DPL position worsens. This is not the primary comparison, but it matters for
latent reading demand.

| Catchment sensitivity | Population | Service points per 1M | Issues per 1M | Reading-room attendance per 1M | PPP spend per resident |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| NCR low | 27,000,000 | 1.48 | 10,176 | 12,417 | $0.60 |
| NCR high | 32,000,000 | 1.25 | 8,586 | 10,477 | $0.50 |

The NCT denominator is therefore the conservative baseline. It does not make
DPL look worse; it makes the comparison administratively fair.

## Data Gaps

DPL reporting now covers many core operational fields, but several IFLA metrics
are still missing or incomplete:

- all physical visits, not only reading-room attendance;
- eBook loans;
- audio-book loans;
- downloads;
- libraries with internet access;
- full-time staff in IFLA-compatible form;
- volunteers;
- digital sessions, public computers, Wi-Fi sessions, and programme attendance.

TPL's current public pages expose richer digital, programme, and branch-visit
data, but do not expose total registered users in the same way DPL reports
membership. The report therefore compares TPL new card registrations separately
and does not pretend they are equivalent to DPL registered-member stock.

## Working Conclusions

1. DPL should be compared on NCT, not NCR, for the main service-area baseline.
2. Even on the conservative NCT denominator, DPL's service density, borrowing,
   collection density, materials spending, and collection renewal are far below
   Toronto's.
3. DPL's current problem is both under-resourcing and low conversion of existing
   stock into public use.
4. Grant dependence is normal for a public library. The red flag is that 98%
   grant-funded operations produce extremely low per-capita use and very low
   materials renewal.
5. The next Delhi extraction should prioritize full DPL annual reports, branch
   locations, service hours, digital services, programmes, and staff deployment
   by branch so the IFLA frame can be completed.
